rows.stem:
In the plot of molar conductivity (\(\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\)) Vs. square root of concentration \((\sqrt{\mathrm{C}})\), following curves are obtained for two electrolytes X and Y :
Answer the following :
(i) Predict the nature of electrolyte X and Y.
(ii) What happens on extrapolation of \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) to concentration approaching zero for electrolytes X and Y ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the question is entirely a reading of the printed graph. Drawn: a first-quadrant plot, y-axis labelled with the molar-conductivity symbol and an upward arrow, x-axis labelled √C with a rightward arrow, carrying TWO unlabelled-origin curves whose right-hand ends are labelled X (upper) and Y (lower). The SHAPES of the two curves are deliberately withheld from this note and from the stem, because 'predict the nature of electrolyte X and Y' is answered by exactly that difference. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
(i) X is a STRONG electrolyte and Y is a WEAK electrolyte.

The SHAPE of the curve is what identifies each. Curve X falls only gently and is very nearly a STRAIGHT LINE — the mark of a strong electrolyte, which is fully dissociated at every dilution, so the small rise in molar conductivity on dilution comes only from the ions interfering with one another's movement less as they move apart.

Curve Y rises STEEPLY towards the vertical axis as the concentration approaches zero. That is the mark of a weak electrolyte, where the DEGREE OF DISSOCIATION itself is increasing, so one mole of electrolyte furnishes more and more ions.

(ii) Curve X CAN be extrapolated to the vertical axis, and the intercept gives \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) directly — this is the standard way of finding the limiting molar conductivity of a strong electrolyte.

Curve Y CANNOT. Near infinite dilution it runs almost PARALLEL to the vertical axis, rising without approaching any limit that can be read off, so there is no intercept to extrapolate to and no \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) is obtained.

For a weak electrolyte the limiting value must therefore be found INDIRECTLY, from KOHLRAUSCH'S LAW — by adding the limiting molar conductivities of its individual ions, each obtained from strong electrolytes that do give a straight line.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: What do you mean by complex reactions ? Can we determine order and molecularity of a complex reaction ?
rows.solution:
A COMPLEX REACTION is one that does NOT occur in a single step. It proceeds through a SEQUENCE of elementary reactions, and the overall balanced equation describes only the net change, not what actually happens at the molecular level.

ORDER — YES, it CAN be determined. Order is an EXPERIMENTAL quantity, read off the measured rate law, so it can be found for any reaction whose rate can be measured. It is governed by the SLOWEST step, and it may come out zero, fractional or even negative, because it need not match the stoichiometry.

MOLECULARITY — NO, it has NO MEANING for a complex reaction.

Molecularity counts the species that must COLLIDE SIMULTANEOUSLY in a SINGLE elementary step, so it is defined only for such a step. Each step of a complex reaction may have its own molecularity, but the sequence as a whole has none to quote — there is no one collision to count.

The two coincide only for an ELEMENTARY reaction, where the step IS the reaction. That is the whole distinction: order is measured and applies to everything; molecularity is theoretical and applies only to a single step.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Account for the following :
(i) Zr and Hf have almost similar atomic radii.
(ii) Transition metals show variable oxidation states.
(iii) Zinc has lowest enthalpy of atomisation.
rows.solution:
(i) Because of the LANTHANOID CONTRACTION.

Hafnium lies a whole period below zirconium, so it should be substantially larger. It is not — both have radii of about 160 pm.

The reason is the fourteen LANTHANOIDS that intervene between them. Across that series each added electron enters an inner \(4f\) orbital, which shields the outer electrons poorly, so the rising nuclear charge pulls the outer shells inwards. The cumulative contraction almost exactly cancels the increase in size expected from the extra period.

The consequence is that zirconium and hafnium behave so alike that they occur together in nature and are notoriously difficult to separate.

(ii) Because the \((n-1)d\) and \(ns\) ORBITALS LIE CLOSE IN ENERGY, so both sets of electrons are available for bonding.

In a main-group metal only the outermost \(s\) and \(p\) electrons are within reach, and the ones below are far too tightly held. In a transition metal the \(3d\) and \(4s\) levels are so nearly equal that electrons can be removed from either, and in varying numbers.

Manganese is the extreme case, reaching every state from \(+2\) to \(+7\), the maximum using all two \(4s\) electrons and all five unpaired \(3d\) electrons.

(iii) Because zinc has a COMPLETELY FILLED \(3d\) subshell, so its d electrons take no part in metallic bonding.

The enthalpy of atomisation measures the strength of the bond holding the metal lattice together, and in the transition series that bond is strengthened by every UNPAIRED d electron contributed to it. Zinc is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{10} 4s^2\) — every d electron paired and held tightly to its own atom — so only the two \(4s\) electrons are available.

With the weakest metallic bond in the series, zinc has the lowest enthalpy of atomisation, and the lowest melting and boiling points.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: Why transition metals and their compounds act as good catalyst ? How is the variability in oxidation states of transition metals different from that of the non-transition metals ? Illustrate with examples.
rows.solution:
TRANSITION METALS ACT AS GOOD CATALYSTS because of their VARIABLE OXIDATION STATES and their ability to form INTERMEDIATE compounds.

A catalyst works by offering a path of lower activation energy, and a transition metal does this by accepting electrons from one reactant and passing them to another — changing oxidation state as it goes, then returning to its original state so that it is not consumed. Vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact process cycles between \(+5\) and \(+4\) in exactly this way.

Finely divided transition metals also provide a large SURFACE on which reactant molecules are ADSORBED and held close together with their bonds weakened, as iron does in the Haber process.

THE DIFFERENCE IN VARIABILITY: transition metals show states differing by ONE unit; non-transition metals show states differing by TWO.

TRANSITION METALS — the \((n-1)d\) and \(ns\) electrons are close in energy and are removed ONE AT A TIME, so consecutive states appear. Manganese gives \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\), \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\), \(\mathrm{Mn^{4+}}\), \(\mathrm{Mn^{6+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Mn^{7+}}\); iron gives \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\).

NON-TRANSITION METALS — their variability comes from the INERT PAIR EFFECT, in which the outer \(s\) PAIR is either retained in full or lost in full, so the states differ by two. Tin gives \(\mathrm{Sn^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Sn^{4+}}\); lead gives \(\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Pb^{4+}}\); no \(+3\) state of either is seen.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Following ions of 3d transition series are given :
\(\mathrm{Ti^{2+}}\), \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\), \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\), \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\)
(Atomic number : Ti = 22, Fe = 26, Cu = 29, Zn = 30)
Identify the ion, which is
(i) a strong reducing agent in aqueous solution.
(ii) more stable than its +1 oxidation state.
(iii) colourless in aqueous solution.
Give a suitable reason in each.
rows.solution:
Work out each configuration first:
\(\mathrm{Ti^{2+}} = 3d^2\), \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}} = 3d^6\), \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}} = 3d^9\), \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}} = 3d^{10}\)

(i) STRONG REDUCING AGENT in aqueous solution: \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\).

A reducing agent gives up an electron readily. Iron(II) is \(3d^6\) — ONE electron beyond the stable half-filled set — and losing that electron gives \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\), which is \(3d^5\), with every orbital singly occupied and the spins parallel. Iron(II) is therefore strongly inclined to be oxidised, which is why a solution of an iron(II) salt turns yellow-brown in air and must be prepared fresh.

(ii) MORE STABLE than its \(+1\) oxidation state: \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\).

The comparison turns on HYDRATION ENTHALPY. The copper(II) ion is smaller and doubly charged, so water binds to it far more strongly than to copper(I) — enough to more than pay for the second ionisation energy. Copper(I) in water therefore DISPROPORTIONATES:
\(2\mathrm{Cu^+(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)} + \mathrm{Cu(s)}\)

In the SOLID state, with no water to hydrate anything, copper(I) compounds are perfectly stable — so the instability belongs to the aqueous solution, not to the ion as such.

(iii) COLOURLESS in aqueous solution: \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\).

Colour arises from a D-D TRANSITION, an electron absorbing visible light and jumping from the lower set of d orbitals to the upper. Zinc(II) is \(3d^{10}\) — COMPLETELY FULL, with no vacancy anywhere to jump into — so no such transition is possible.

The other three all have both electrons and vacancies: titanium(II) is violet, iron(II) green and copper(II) blue.
